utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Registrar, kindly call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-03-67-T, the Prosecutor versus Vojislav Seselj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Madam Registrar. Today is Tuesday, the 4th of November, 2008. Good morning to the OTP representatives, to Mr. Mundis and Mr. Dutertre, good morning to their team, and good morning to Mr. Seselj. Good morning to all the people helping us. I can tell you straight away that we will stop today at five to 1.00, because at 1.00 the President of this Tribunal is going to be elected. This is the reason why we shall stop today at five to 1.00. I also wanted to ask this of the Prosecution, and later on I'll put the question to Mr. Seselj: We seek a clarification regarding Davor Strinovic. Regarding his testimony, the Trial Chamber has been seized of two motions: One of the 13th of July, 2006; the other dated 18th of September, 2008. "Mr. Seselj," I was going to say. Mr. Mundis, you're on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Just in anticipation of whatever question or clarification Your Honour was going to put to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So just wait before you answer, because this is going to be a long question. We have two motions: One of the 13th of July, 2006; the other being of the 18th of September, 2008. There are several attachments or schedules to these motions with basically the same documents, seeking for them to be tendered. These exhibits were tendered and admitted in the Milosevic and Mrksic cases, but their legal foundation is not the same, either it's the former 92 bis (D), a basis of foundation that was changed to 92 ter by the Prosecution, or is it a 94(B). The question before the Trial Chamber is as follows: Does the Prosecution request admission on the sole foundation of 94(B) or is the Prosecution's motion based on both Rules on an alternative base? If it's too complicated right now, you can give an answer later on, another day, but this is the question I wanted to put to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours, to the accused, and to everyone in and around the courtroom. We would be proceeding on the basis of an alternative formulation, so 94(B) or, in the alternative, 92 bis (D). Let me also, while I'm on my feet, with respect to this witness indicate and flag up, we're in the final stages of trying to add a few witnesses for the next few weeks, in order to make sure that the schedule proceeds as smoothly as possible. Professor Strinovic has agreed to travel to The Hague on the 9th of November and to testify on the 11th of November, which is one week from today. I will be confirming all of that and putting it in writing to the Trial Chamber and to Dr. Seselj, but it is our intention at this stage to bring Professor Strinovic next week, barring any unforeseen circumstances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, this gives me an opportunity to ask this of Dr. Seselj: Mr. Seselj, on the 2nd of October, 2008, you received the translation into B/C/S, into your language, of the motion of the 18th of September, 2008. Do you plan to file a response to that motion of the 18th of September, 2008, whilst the deadline, the time limit of 14 days, has already past?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have several things which I should like to tell you. First of all, I have no intention of responding in writing to that motion, because all communication with my legal advisers has been severed. Secondly, I cannot, in fact, recall in essence the content of that motion because it was submitted to me a month or so ago. Thirdly, I do not believe that there is anything of the essence in there on account of which I would have to state my view in order to facilitate your situation. Fourthly, I should just like to point to the action of the OTP. Dr. Strinovic was announced for the 25th of November, and now he's being announced for the next week. This is unfair. I have nothing against it. I am prepared for Davor Strinovic for the next week, but I have to say that this is an unfair proceeding. And, fifthly, and most importantly, if we are talking about documents that have been tendered in other cases, then it didn't cost the OTP anything to adapt those documents to this particular case, to designate them numbers within this case, and to find them as such -- tender them as such, rather than have me investigating other cases. If we are talking about hearings in other cases and the transcripts being admitted, then I'm adamantly against that, because no Defence in any other case can coincide with the thesis of my own Defence, aside the fact that I consider many he Defences in this Tribunal to be incompetent, that they actually operated to the detriment of the accused, and that they work with some instructions or factors which cannot be clearly and precisely identified but certainly do exist. So as the expert report of Davor Strinovic actually no way collaborates the OTP's thesis against me, as it deals with autopsies of victims of crimes, which are, of course, indubitable, it can be useful for certain thesis of the Defence. You will see, although there have been some witnesses who have falsely claimed here that some victims have been killed with cold steel, that some weapons that have not been used have been used, the expert can tell us whether there really had been victims that died of cold steel, whether a 357 magnum revolver ammunition had been used, et cetera. Of course, that can be useful, but it has to be viva voce testimony, because evidence tendered in other cases has to be adapted to this case and be tendered as an addition under 65 ter, while it is out of the question for transcripts of the hearings of these witnesses in other cases to be admitted or to be accepted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Regarding this last point, Mr. Seselj, admittedly this expert witness was scheduled for the 25th of November, but you know that we have run into scheduling problems which are connected with the fact that some witnesses that were scheduled are not going to appear or have disappeared. We have to adjust to the circumstances, and this is the reason why Mr. Strinovic has been put forward and is going to testify on the 11th of November. This being said, regarding the issue of exhibits, I listened to you with great care. At first blush, as far as I'm concerned, at least, I agree with you. The fact that exhibits were admitted in other cases does not automatically mean that they have to be admitted here. We have Rule 94(B) that says clearly that ex officio, or upon the request of parties and after hearing the parties, the Trial Chamber may decide to take judicial notice of facts or documentary evidence admitted in other cases brought before the Tribunal connected to the instant case. It so happens that the Milosevic case was not completed. This is a very special case, and the Mrksic case at appeal stage. Therefore, we're going to have the expert witness. No doubt the Prosecutor is going to submit documents probably coming from the Milosevic and Mrksic cases. You are going to cross-examine the witness. There's going to be questions by the Judges. So we will rule on the admission of exhibits in the final stage, after all the other procedural steps. So this is what I wanted to convey to you. Dr. Seselj, I think you had something else to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but beforehand, I need to ask this of the accused: Could you be more specific when you refer to the issue of disclosure? You say that privileged disclosure was interrupted, not disclosure or communication in a general way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, did you have other housekeeping matters?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I have two other administrative issues to raise. Upon returning from the court on the 29th of October, in the evening, I received a new letter from the Registrar, informing me that the severance of communication with my legal advisers has been extended by another month. Communication with the legal advisers, Judge Lattanzi, can be privileged or it can be nonexistent. There is not a civilised state in this world where anyone can, in fact, listen in on the conversations of an accused with members of his Defence team, at least I know of no such state. But I've been here for quite a long time, six years. Perhaps things have changed. The world has changed substantially. This globalism as the new totalitarianism has made headway in many countries. Here, the Registrar first invokes the information that he had available, which is exclusively statements of Tomislav Nikolic given to the Serbian media, to the effect that I had used this privileged communication line with my legal advisers to conduct political talks with my collaborators and to give them political instructions. That is repeated in this second paragraph of the Registrar's decision. And the Registrar also finds fault with me because I am using that telephone for things which are not connected with the preparation of my Defence; that is to say, the Registrar takes Tomislav Nikolic's word for it. So Tomislav Nikolic has become, of late, the pit of America, et cetera --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, please. If I'm not mistaken, you yourself said during a hearing, and please correct me if I'm wrong, you said that through this privileged line, you spoke to associates that were other associates than those who enjoy a privileged status. Am I wrong?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, you are not wrong. I was given just one single telephone number to use it in privileged communication. That is the telephone number of the office of my legal adviser/lawyer Slavko Jerkovic. I was never able to call my other legal advisers using that telephone, but I sit here in the courtroom. Whenever I was to make a call, I would inform them in advance that I would be making that call, so that the other legal advisers would be there and the other members of my Defence team as well; my investigators, in other words, as well as other legal advisers who have not been registered here. However, on several occasions, by a special submission, I informed the Registrar who the team members for my Defence were; and in each of my submissions to the Trial Chamber, I listed names on the cover page. So no one can actually deny me the right to be -- keep in touch with them and to give them tasks in terms of what they are to do in the field in order to obtain certain facts, information, or documents which are of the essence for my Defence. I should like to remind you, Madam Lattanzi, that my predecessor in the exercise of this right to defend himself, Mr. Slobodan Milosevic, had available a separate office for his use, which I do not have. I do not have one. He had a special telephone line which only he used. I don't have one. Thirdly, Mr. Milosevic - and I'm an eyewitness to that because I saw him three or four times when my testimony was being prepared - could call literally whomever he pleased using that telephone line. So the restrictions placed on me are much, much harsher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, I have a question in this respect. Did you file a request with the Registry for leave to use a privileged line with those of your associates who did not enjoy a privileged status? Have you made the request for leave to use another line with those people? Have you done anything to be able to extend the use of that line? I don't know, maybe it would have been possible to get something else, something extra. But have you made the request; and if you did ask, we need to know that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Lattanzi, I've done so repeatedly on several occasions throughout 2007. The President of the Trial Chamber, Judge Antonetti, was the Pre-Trial Judge. He even asked that a telephone line and a fax be installed in my cell so that I could receive fax messages during the night as well, and the Registry responded that it was impossible because other convicts in Scheveningen could use the telephone in my cell. That was the response I received. So these are questions which have been thrashed out innumerable times at innumerable Status Conferences throughout 2007. In the end, it all boiled down to this: I am able to just dial one telephone line, telephone number, and that the privileged telephone set is in the corridor. So when I make a call, all the convicts which are in that part of the unit can hear my conversation. I have a quite loud voice, I'm not used to whispering, and the cells are right there, and I'm making the calls right outside their cells. I have reconciled myself to that situation. I used that particular line, but now I am left even without that. Why am I insisting on this so much? I have my reasons. The basic argumentation of my Defence in my concluding remarks will be that this is an irregular trial because of this, this, and that. One of the reasons will be this that we are talking about. It is for me to warn you of this. It is up to you to see to the fairness of the trial. It is not for me to see to the fairness of the trial. In fact, it is in my interest for this trial to be objectively unfair for every neutral observer. It is not enough for justice to be done. It has to be seen that justice is being done. That is the essence. The second argument which has to do with this decision of the Registrar, if you will allow me. Can I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Registrar also said that he is to consider the serious claims of harassment or intimidation which are contained in a number of submissions to be considered to be discussed by the Trial Chamber. In fact, what the Registrar is doing, he's using the OTP submissions, which have not been ruled on yet, in order to substantiate his decision to sever my communication because ostensibly I have intimidated people. The Registrar has also objections to the fact that my advisers, my collaborators, are my long hand. So what? That is only normal. I was not in a single location during the actual commission of the crimes. I, as a rule, do not know these concrete perpetrators. How can I defend myself if I do not talk have my investigators and if do not communicate with my investigators? Although I demanded in writing to be able to be visited by investigators, this has never been granted me. I actually only gained the right to legal advisers visits in 2006, after five years of staying here. Towards the end of the first page, the Registrar utters this threat. He says: "If proceedings for contempt of court or disciplinary proceedings are instituted against my legal advisers, he can decide to actually revoke their appointments." These are just empty threats. These are threats, but these are empty threats. But if he revokes them, I will not do that, because they will remain my legal advisers until I lose confidence in them and I revoke them. I will not have the Registrar revoking them. They're used to this in other cases, and the basic problem of this Tribunal is the that Tribunal is paying for the lawyers, and the lawyers are not working in the interests of the accused but in the interests of the Registry, the OTP, et cetera. That is why many defences are non-starters here. This is the first time the Registrar is coming across a serious defence, and I consider myself a serious defence and superior in respect of all other lawyers who work here, because in contrast to them, I know how much -- how to defend myself and I do not shirk from really saying what I think at every moment, and they do. Their mouths can be shut by a threat of the Presiding Judge or by a frown on the face of the acting OTP representative. There have been numerous examples in this Tribunal of that, and I can quote them from the practice of Toma Fila and on. That is as far as the Registrar's decision is concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, we know all this. I shall answer to part of what you said, but could you please finish and formulate your request?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the first question. I have another question to raise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, as to the first question regarding communication, last time you put this issue to the Trial Chamber following the decision made by the Registrar. He extended, by another 30 days, his decision based, so it seems, but I haven't read the decision yet, based on the fact that allegedly Mr. Nikolic said that you used the line for other purposes than your defence and, secondly, also on the basis of other proceedings. Last time I told you that this Trial Chamber would hand down a decision following your oral request. I shall speak about it with my colleagues for that to be done very quickly. Indeed, as a Judge, when I hear you say that this is an unfair trial, that's like an electroshock to me. So this decision will say very quickly, as a Trial Chamber or as an individual opinion, will say exactly the problem that is raised by communication between an accused and his advisers or associates. So we have taken due note of what you said. Of course, the Trial Chamber will have to give you an answer, but you know this as well as I do. You can also challenge this with the President of the Tribunal. You can challenge the decision made by the Registrar. That's the first thing. Now, what was the second thing you wanted to say?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is something that is just now being prepared in the Registry against me, but I have reliable information about it; and in my eyes, it is a much greater danger than what is happening currently. Under the instructions of the US and British intelligence services, Aleksandar Vucic and Tomislav Nikolic have been, for quite a while, campaigning in Belgrade against me, stating that I had ordered their liquidation or that I had instructed the activists of my Serbian Radical Party to cause bloodshed at their rallies. The Yellow Press in Belgrade has been writing about it for days, as well as certain media under the influence of Serbian tycoons. You're probably familiar with this because you are following the reporting concerning this trial. What is the point? The point is to create in the public the impression that I'm really endangering someone's life.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry, my mic was not on. What does the Registrar have to do with all this, with this press campaign that you're now mentioning?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They have something to do with it, because the Registrar is getting ready to use this campaign, led by Aleksandar Vucic and Tomislav Nikolic, to write a new decision prohibiting all further family or other visits to me. For seven months in end 2003 and early 2004, the Registrar had already done this; and again for two months on a later occasion, they prohibited all telephone communications and family visits to me under the pretext that I'm intimidating or endangering the life of some people. Then they used it to prepare a submission, a motion to impose counsel on me, and I am not able to effectively represent myself unless I have the cooperation of my advisers. That is the point of the conspiracy. I'm no paranoid. I'm just a person with enormous political experience who is perfectly able to draw conclusions from the moves made against me. And as for the campaign, I'm sure you're aware of it. He ordered bloodshed to be caused, he ordered a contract killing, et cetera, et cetera. All those who have so far accused me of jeopardising anyone's life had no evidence whatsoever. They said I endangered the life of some witnesses. Who? Albanians killed some witnesses off and nobody made a move, nobody lifted a finger in this Tribunal. There were a couple of witnesses here who only claimed somebody was harassing them by phone, and that was so transparent, it was ridiculous. What would be my interest in harassing a witness or intimidating them, when I'm so superior to all of them? I want to triumph in this trial, and I will. Whatever the judgement, the triumph will be mine, I assure you. But I draw your attention to what is going on, because this trial is being supervised by the US and British intelligence services very closely because of their strategic interests in the Balkans. I have been here for six years now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, I read in the newspapers articles related to Mr. Vucic and Mr. Nikolic. I believe that a rally was supposed to take place and that it was cancelled at the very last minute. From what I read in the paper, investigations are underway, but it's up to local authorities to try to shed some light on this matter. Now, with respect to the impact of what took place there on your visits, now that's a different kettle of fish altogether. I do not know exactly what the Registrar will do about this. If the Registrar makes an administrative decision, you can challenge it with the President of the Tribunal, if you believe that it endangers your defence. You can also refer the matter to the Trial Chamber. I've always repeated that presumption of innocence is the rule, the absolute rule. And as far as I'm concerned, I do not see why you should be forbidden from meeting with your wife. So what you should do now is to see what will happen, and we're going to have the witness brought in now. But before doing so, let me turn to the OTP. We learned that on the 3rd of November, you sent a letter to Mr. Seselj, telling him that you were disclosing a number of documents under Rule 68(I). These are exculpatory documents. You explained that you found these documents at the last minute and that because of that, you could not provide a translation. Is it really what happened yesterday, Mr. Dutertre?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, Mr. Seselj. Last night, in a letter copied to the Chamber, we explained to Mr. Seselj that a number of 68 documents related to Dr. Bosanac have not been translated into B/C/S. As a result, so far, these documents have not been disclosed to Mr. Seselj. We have attached the list of the relevant documents to the letter, and everyone can have an idea about the nature of these documents and about the number of documents we are talking about. Because of scheduling problems you referred to yourself, Your Honour, we decided nonetheless to have Dr. Bosanac testify today. Of course, the OTP has no qualms about Dr. Bosanac being called back to testify again, once the documents have been disclosed to Mr. Seselj, and if he believes he has questions to put to her on the basis of these documents. We believe that the rights of Mr. Seselj are protected here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you tell us, document by document, Mr. Dutertre, which documents could be relevant? That way, things will be much clearer.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With respect to exculpatory documents, the OTP has a very broad understanding of this decision -- of this definition. We disclose everything that could be used by the Defence. So, in that list, you will find a large variety of documents. Sometimes it's not very clear whether the document is exculpatory or not, but if there is a doubt in that matter, then we classify it under Rule 68. From memory, it would be a bit tricky for me to tell you, for each document, whether it is more relevant or not. What happens is that over these past few weeks, Mr. Seselj has received a number of documents under Rule 66, 66(B), and 68, and the information contained in the documents that have not been disclosed are already to be found in the disclosed documents. In other words, Mr. Seselj already has at his disposal most of the exculpatory data related to Ms. Bosanac, but we always want to be as comprehensive as possible. That's why we want to disclose all relevant documents, but because of translation delays, we have not been able to do so yet. It's only on the 23rd of October that we received a revised translation of these -- of some of these documents, and then we had to deal with all documents related to VS-034. That complicated matters in terms of disclosure of all these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Whilst listening to you, I was adding up all these documents. We have 38 documents in total. Some documents are books, press articles. We have something coming from the BBC. That's one type of document. I can see that we have documents coming from the Red Cross. We have a document that was exhibited in the Mrksic case, Exhibit 867. So, yes, indeed, we are talking about a large variety of documents. Mr. Seselj, you will study that list. I am unable to tell you what the content of the documents is. The OTP adopted a very broad approach when disclosing these documents to you. They believe that they might be of some relevance for your Defence. I can see that the document number 2 comes from the 49th Session of the Human Rights Commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We always indicate the number of pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. These documents could be relevant for your Defence. When it comes to the witness we're going to hear just now, one or two documents may be relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Dutertre, why are these documents being disclosed so late?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Dr. Bosanac is extremely well known. Everybody knows her. She stayed in the Vukovar Hospital until the very end. She's mentioned in a huge number of documents. You have hundreds of documents classified in various collections, and it took quite a while to process all these documents. All these documents are documents where her name is mentioned once or twice, and it took a very long time to process all these documents. And once we've identified which documents are exculpatory or not, they need to be sent to the Translation Unit, and this makes the matter even more cumbersome. A number of articles were written about this witness. She was mentioned in various testimonies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, would you have a brief comment about all this?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I think the Trial Chamber should not tolerate such actions of the Prosecution. I'm surprised that one of the untranslated documents is the book of Mate Granic. As far as I know, the book of Mate Granic was originally published in Serbian; not a very good Serbian, of course, the somewhat artificial Serbian nowadays published in Croatia. But there's no need to translate it, anyway. Now, look at the fifth or sixth line from the bottom, that's it. What is more important, Vesna Bosanac, because of her essential role in the war events in Vukovar, is one of the key witnesses in this trial. That is why my rights to due process are considerably prejudiced by introducing Vesna Bosanac as a 92 ter witness. Since you granted her that status, despite my objection, you know in advance that I'm not going to cross-examine her, so this discussion is completely out of place. I will never agree that any witness here can appear as 92 ter, because that Rule was introduced after February 2003 and it cannot be applied retroactively. I don't understand why you decided to apply it that way. I am completely not interested in the testimony of Vesna Bosanac or any other 92 ter witness. Obviously, we have nothing to do tomorrow and the day after tomorrow. I will address the Prosecution with a motion that all this time be deducted from their time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, the Trial Chamber has read the statement taken on the 23rd of September from this witness, and we looked through the statement very carefully to see if there's anything that could incriminate you, directly or indirectly, in the statement. If that had been the case, then we would have decided that the witness had to be cross-examined. The written statement is organised in the following manner: There's the first part of the testimony dedicated to the personal background of the witness, the studies, and the fact that she was appointed director; then we have a second part dedicated to the Vukovar population, to the blockade, to the situation in town; and then we have something dedicated to the bombing of the town. Apparently, you were not the one who ordered this shelling, unless you tell us that it was you, of course. Then we move on to the 17th of November, 1991, to the 18th of November, 1991, to the 19th of November, 1991. After that, we have a portion dedicated to the 20th of November. We have two sections dedicated to her detention because she was arrested. Then we have a section on the lists of victims, and then we have a section related to documents, to new documents. The only very remote link with you, possibly, is the fact that at some point, she mentions Chetniks. At no point does she mention volunteers from the Serb Radical Party in her statement. Furthermore, and we'll see it when I ask questions later on, this witness has testified in a number of cases here at the Tribunal. She testified in the Mrksic case for six days. So this statement seems to be a sort of summary of all the things she said previously or she stated previously in various trials. You decided not to cross-examine her. That's your choice. I am personally going to put questions to her, because there's a great deal of things that I find rather unclear; in other words, everything that happened before the town was put under blockade by the JNA. I have a great deal of questions to put to her about this specific period, and I have questions to put to her about the way events unfolded. We are going to have the witness brought in and ask her to take the solemn declaration. Mr. Dutertre.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know if you want us to do this -- or to deal with this before the document comes into the courtroom. I have an application to make to add five documents to the 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the 3rd of October, the Prosecution filed a motion for the admission of the 92 ter statement from Dr. Bosanac. At that time, we stated that we had received, on the 23rd of September, 2008, three documents from Ms. Bosanac, three documents in B/C/S, and the translation of these documents was underway. Of course, these documents were disclosed to the accused. Since then, we have received the English translation of these documents, and the OTP is now requesting for these documents to be added to the 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please identify the numbers of these documents and their titles?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The first document is a document that bears a provisional 65 ter number: ERN number 0641-9452 - 0641-9456, provisional 65 ter number 7340. The title is -- well, actually, it's a list of 193 identified persons from the grave, from the grave at Ovcara or the mass grave at Ovcara. This is the last updated list that Ms. Bosanac received from the Croatian authorities by a fax that was sent to her in August 2008, if memory serves me right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The second document.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The second document is a document that has the ERN number 0641-9449 - 0641-9451, provisional 65 ter number 7341. This is a list of 97 individuals found in the Ovcara grave, and the witness has established that these people were also at the hospital. The third document, documents given to us by Dr. Bosanac, ERN number 0641-9457 - 0641-9549, provisional 65 ter number 7342. These are death certificates, several death certificates. These documents were disclosed to the accused on the 2nd of October, 2008.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fourth document.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have two documents left, Your Honour. We have one document which is a fax dated 3rd of November, 1991, ERN number 0117-2530, provisional 65 ter number 7338, disclosed to the accused on the 9th of July, 2008. The last document, it's the Zagreb evacuation agreement signed on the 18th of November, 1991, ERN number 0007-2600, provisional 65 ter number 7339, and this document was also disclosed to the accused on the 9th of July, 2008.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What about this last document, this Zagreb evacuation agreement, wasn't it exhibited in the Mrksic case?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, absolutely, Your Honour, but let me check this. Yes, I believe you're right, and we overlooked this document when we requested an amendment of the list of exhibits on the 4th of April, 2008.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, what do you have to say about these five documents added to the 65 ter list?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have absolutely no interest whatsoever in these documents and the issue itself, but let me draw your attention to the fact that Vesna Bosanac testified for six days in the Mrksic case, and that tells you how important she is as a witness. She is just going to go -- come in and out into this courtroom, and that will be the end of it. She does not incriminate me, personally, but she and the next witness are so important for discovering the truth and the background of the crime in Ovcara that it is absolutely incomprehensible to me how these witnesses can be simply introduced as 92 ter. I don't see which witnesses could possibly be more important than Vesna Bosanac and the next one who is protected, so I'm not going to mention his name. I don't see any other witnesses testifying about Ovcara here. These are the two most important ones, but that's your decision, and what can I do about it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let's have the witness brought in. Mr. Usher, can you go and fetch the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, should I understand that these documents have been admitted with the 65 ter numbers suggested by the OTP?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Trial Chamber has decided that these documents should be added to the 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, madam. Could you please state your first name, last name, and date of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. My name is Vesna Bosanac. I was born on the 9th of March, 1949, in Subotica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your current occupation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am a physician. Right now, I am the administrator of the general hospital in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Have you ever testified before this Tribunal or before a national court; and if that's the case, can you please identify the cases in which you've testified?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I testified before this Tribunal in the trial against Dokmanovic, against Slobodan Milosevic, against Sljivancanin, Mrksic, and Radic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the first case you've just mentioned, in the Dokmanovic case, for how many days did you testify?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Two days, I believe. I'm not sure. It was quite a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And what about the Milosevic case, how long did your testimony last?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Two days, but I did come twice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And in the Mrksic case, how long did you testify in that case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think I testified for five days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And if I were to tell you that you testified during six days in that case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I remember that I spent six days here, but I'm not sure that I really testified for six days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Did you testify before national courts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please tell me before which court you testified and in what case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, I gave a statement before an investigating judge in Osijek, and that was back in 1992 and 1993; and last year, I testified about Vukovar in Vukovar, in the trial against Bogdan Kuzmic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Please read the solemn declaration, Madam.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. You may be seated. Let me give you some information about the way we are going to proceed in this case. The Trial Chamber, after receiving a relevant application from the OTP, decided to hear your testimony under Rule 92 ter. In other words, contrary to what happened in your testimonies in the Milosevic and Dokmanovic case, you won't be a viva voce testimony in this case, but the Prosecutor will put questions to you based on a written statement taken on the 23rd of September, 2008, a written statement signed by yourself. The Prosecution will also submit a number of documents to you. After that, the Judges will put questions to you, and I believe that I will put a large number of questions to you with respect to the contents of your written statement and also what's not to be found in your written statement and should have been there, in my opinion. The accused in this case, Mr. Seselj, has stated that he does not wish to cross-examine you, not because it's you, but because, as a matter of principle, he's opposed to the 92 ter procedure. That's the reason why he has decided not to cross-examine you. But we have to specify here that in his view, you are a very relevant witness. You're scheduled to testify over two days. We might be done today, but that would surprise me. Normally, we should continue with your testimony tomorrow. You are a witness who's about to testify to the events in Vukovar. Everybody is aware of this. You lost two members of your family, including your own father, in the events. This must be kept in everybody's mind. We break every 90 minutes. We started this hearing at 8.30, so we'll stop for our first break at 10.00 this morning, and we shall finish the proceedings today at five to 1.00 because the Judges have a meeting at 1.00. The President of this Tribunal is going to be elected. This is the reason why we stop earlier than usual. We'll have a break at 10.00. We shall resume at 10.20 to continue for another 90 minutes. If at any time you would like to have a break for any reason whatsoever, just say so and I will, of course, make sure we have a break for you to have a rest if you need -- if you feel you need one. This is what I wanted to tell you, Madam. This is a 92 ter witness, so you'll read out your usual summary, and then you'll carry on with the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Actually, in order to save time and in view of the number of exhibits to submit to this witness, I'm not going to read out a summary. I'll go straight to the questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but do tell us, in a few words, what the witness is going to testify to so that the people who follow us outside this courtroom know what the object of this testimony will be.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will proceed. This witness was appointed director of the Vukovar Hospital in July 1991. This witness organised the hospital services in Vukovar during the conflict, right up to the 20th of November, 1991, when she was detained by the Serbian authorities. This witness, therefore, has information as to the situation in Vukovar throughout the conflict. She can give you information as to the situation in the hospital during the conflict, the material conditions in the hospital for the patients, and the way people could do their work. The witness is going to provide information regarding the very last days before the fall of the town on the 17th, the 18th, 19th and 20th of November, 1991. She can speak to the influx of population to the hospital. The people sought shelter because there was an appeal to evacuation. The population was aware of it. This is the reason why the OTP wanted to add this witness to the witness list in April, because Dr. Bosanac mainly can make the link between the list of people present in the hospital and some individuals that were found in the Ovcara grave. This is the main point of her testimony for us. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we've prepared two binders with exhibits, and we shall ask the witness to have a look at them in the binders, rather than using the e-court, in order to save some time. We can spare some seconds every time, but of course I'll give you the 65 ter numbers. Everybody's received the binders, including the accused. There may be a document, a coloured document, that we haven't put in the binders, but we'll give it at the right time. Let's first have the 92 ter statement of Dr. Bosanac. We gave it the number 7343.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Dr. Bosanac, you have on the desk the two binders I just mentioned. There may be some loose sheets. They show the statement you gave in September. Maybe you could have the help of the usher for you to find the right document. I'm speaking about your interview of the 23rd of September, 2008. That should be found in the first binder. Do you have the document, Doctor?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Dr. Bosanac, is this the statement you signed on the 23rd of September, 2008?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Is this written statement a true reflection of what you said?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Third question, Dr. Bosanac: If you were to answer the same questions, would you say the same thing?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I seek to tender 65 ter number 7343, and then we can move on to the other exhibits that I will also seek to tender.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Registrar, can we have a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will become Exhibit number P587.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Now, right at the beginning of the binder, you have a chart showing the exhibits, the ERN numbers, a description, and the paragraph in English, the relevant paragraphs. I shall be very brief when reviewing each document, in order to save time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Dr. Bosanac, let me look at the first document to be found under tab 1 in the binder. That's tab 1. Please take this document mentioned in paragraph 10 of your statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's 65 ter number 7286, 65 ter number 7286.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: We have the version in English and in B/C/S, and you have it in B/C/S. Can you confirm the date, that is, 21st of October, 1991?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Who signed this document?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Just a minute. I have the English version before me here.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Please just go to the previous page and you should have the B/C/S version of the document, so just before the green sheet.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Yes, I've found it. You asked me who wrote this document. I dictated it. It was written by Administrator Verica Graf, and I signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Thank you for this answer. Just say, in a few words, what the contents of the document is.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: This is a letter which I wrote to the European Mission, the Croatian office in Zagreb, in which I described what the situation in the hospital was like. That was immediately after the Medicins Sans Frontieres convey had left the hospital, which had helped us, because it had taken a number of gravely wounded out from the hospital. But the situation remained difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Dr. Bosanac. I seek to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment. I have a question. Madam, this is a letter that was faxed. I see that it is said that this document was sent at 12.35 on the 21st. It says "21/10." Normally, yes, that's 21/10/91; that's the date. But I'm looking at the fax number, or there's a phone number; and underneath, handwritten, we have a fax number. Whose fax number is this? Is that the ECMM's fax office or is it the fax number of the liaison office, the Croatian liaison office?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is the number of the fax which was the Inn Hotel in Zagreb where the seat was of the European Mission, and the Croatian liaison office was there, and that is their number, the one which is handwritten, in Zagreb at the Inn Hotel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We're going to give it a number. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P588, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Dr. Bosanac, can we move on to tab 2.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters request: Can all microphones be switched off, please. We cannot hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation][Previous translation continues]... statement. It is 65 ter number 7296. I'm going to repeat the number. So the document to be found in tab 2, mentioned in paragraph 21 of 65 ter document 7296. It's a very short document.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Can you confirm that it has to do with the events of the 31st of October, 1991?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Who authored the document?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: I am, I am the author. Actually, I told it over the phone. I called on a daily basis the European Mission, the postal centre in Vukovar, which then referred my appeals to other institutions that were relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Thank you. What is this document about? What do you say in this document?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: I'm describing the situation on that day, the 31st of October, 1991, at 1345. The plane again threw two plane bombs on the hospital, on the wounded, on the newborn infants, on the women and the patients, and I'm asking for urgent cessation of attacks on the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I seek to tender this document, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have several questions, Witness. In your language, we have the description of what happened on the 31st of October. You say that a plane dropped two bombs. It is typewritten. This typewritten passage is part, isn't it -- or is it part of a personal notebook, of just loose sheets? How did you go about typewriting this? Did you ask your secretary to type the contents of the phone conversation? Could you give us further details on this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I gave this information over the telephone to the Croatian office attached to the European Mission, via our post office in Vukovar, and through the office to liaising with their post office in Osijek. This is very brief information which I imparted over the phone and then appealed for the firing to stop. At that moment on the 31st of October, I did not give instructions for that to be written down. It was just an oral appeal on my part which I made in this way. And later, when I arrived in Zagreb, in the Croatian -- I found these notes in the Croatian office attached to the European Mission, which then I collected and had published in a book which is called "The Appeals of Dr. Vesna Bosanac."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You can see that a lot of things become clear when a Judge puts questions. You wrote a book entitled "The Appeals of Dr. Vesna Bosanac." If I understand you properly, you had made a phone call in order to describe the event, and then when you went to the offices of the European Mission in Zagreb, you saw some traces of this telephone call you had made, and this became the text that we now can see. In other words, the typewritten text was typewritten well after the event. When was it done; two, three, ten years later? When was it typewritten?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, this was typewritten when it happened, but it was only later that I got hold of that text, after arriving in Zagreb, in fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So it was -- was it typewritten by your secretary when you made the call?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was typed by the person on duty who received this call, who was in the Croatian office attached to the European Mission in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now we've got it. So it was the person on duty who mentioned in this document what you had said to her. At least that is clear now. When you called the European Mission, who did you speak to, who talked to you? Did you speak to a secretary? Did you speak to the person in charge? Who was at the other end of the line?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I spoke to a lady who was in charge of and on duty to receive telephone calls.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Was this person female, the person on duty?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So she wrote down what you said; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's now clear. We're going to give an IC number. An IC number for this document, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: IC 77, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That can't be right. Madam Registrar, we should have a "P" number, and it should be somewhere around -- well, it should be the one following the previous document. It should be 589.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it is 589, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to point out that the book written by Dr. Bosanac was disclosed to the accused under disclosure receipt 464. Let me move on to the third document under tab 3, mentioned in paragraph 22, with a 65 ter number 7299.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Can you confirm the date of this document, is it 2nd of November, 1991?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Who signed this document?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: At the end of the document, it is written: "Message received by liaison officer Alen Kosovic."

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: What do you know of Alen Kosovic?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: I do not know him personally, but at that time, he was the liaison officer at the Croatian office attached to the European Mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Do you remember speaking to Mr. Kosovic on the phone about issues mentioned in this document?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. President, I seek to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're going to give a number, but before we do so: So you phoned Mr. Kosovic and you told him that the hospital was under artillery fire, you described the situation as of that day, you said that there were babies born on that day, and so on and so forth. Then you said that on behalf of the 2.500 children of Vukovar, you were asking for an immediate ceasefire. What did Mr. Kosovic reply? Did he say he was going to forward your request? What did he say, exactly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He told me that he would convey my message.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Who was he going to forward it to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I called the Croatian office, I repeat, attached to the European Mission in Zagreb at the Inn Hotel where their seat, their headquarters, was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but I suppose that there was a head in the European Mission in Zagreb. There's always a head to any service or administration. Obviously, he was not the head, was he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I don't know exactly what his post was. I could see that he was the officer in charge of contacts. In fact, the man at the head of the European Mission was Georges-Marie Chenu, who was in charge of conducting negotiations and who signed the document on the evacuation of the Vukovar Hospital. He was a -- he's a Frenchman; and for a while, he was the French ambassador to Croatia in Zagreb, and I believe that he wrote a book about this entire situation at that time and that I also met him later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So he, too, wrote a book?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you called at 12.30 on that day, on the 2nd of November, 1991, when you made that call, it seems that the situation was rather serious. Why did you not ask to speak personally to this Frenchman whose first name is Georges, but the surname is not in the transcript? Just why didn't you ask to talk to him to forward your request? Why did you not demand from Mr. Kosovic that you could speak to him personally, because it was 12.30. He probably wasn't asleep then. He must have been somewhere.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I tried every day, in really very difficult conditions with shells landing on the hospital incessantly. Almost a thousand shells landed on the hospital every day as well as on the entire town. So I tried on a daily basis to get in touch with anyone relevant enough to help us. Regrettably, sometimes I managed to get in touch with some persons in charge; sometimes I didn't. It wasn't -- simply, it wasn't easy to do under the circumstances. Many people in Vukovar at that time, as well as my associates and colleagues, thought that the job that I was doing was totally pointless, so that we were doomed anyway to destruction and that it was to no avail. I did my very best. Sometimes, I could get in touch with some relevant persons, at least I thought so at that time - I mean, that they were relevant - and, sometimes, I didn't manage to get in touch with anyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, on that day you spoke to Mr. Kosovic, did the Frenchman call you back later to tell you that he was going to go further up to speak to relevant people? If he wasn't relevant in the matter, did he say he was going to try to speak to the JNA? Did he call you back, or did he fail to do anything?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I personally did not get any call. At that time, whether he had tried to do anything, I don't know. I met Mr. Chenu later, several years after the war, and I really don't know what he did at that particular point in time. The only persons who called and tried to do something were the Medecins Sans Frontieres, who tried to help us and who came to Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll get to that later. So he did not call you back. Very well. Let us have a number for the document, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P590, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's now 10.00. We're going to have a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The court is back in session. Mr. Dutertre.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Let's now move on to the fourth document at tab 4, mentioned at paragraph 37, and bearing the following number, 65 ter number 7284, 7284. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Witness, who authored this document, who signed this document?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: I personally signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: What is the date of this document?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: 20th October 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: And why did you send this document to Medecins Sans Frontieres? What was the purpose of this document?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: I wanted to thank them, because they had tried to help us in the hospital. I wanted to express my regret over their nurses who had been wounded in that incident as they were returning. I wanted to invite them to try to help again, because the representative of Medecins Sans Frontieres called me on the phone to say that the nurses had been wounded and that he was afraid he would no longer be able to continue with the process of evacuation, because they had said earlier they would come every other day and evacuate the wounded from the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Witness. I seek to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A very brief question, Witness. This letter was sent to Christopher Besse from MSF, but how did he physically receive that letter? How was the letter supposed to reach him, personally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know whether the letter reached him. I had sent it the same way as I sent everything else, by fax, that I used when sending communications to the Ministry of Health and the Office for Communication of the European Mission in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. On the document, in your own language, I don't see anything related to when the fax was sent or I don't see any fax number, but you're telling us that this document was sent by fax. We'll have a number for this document now.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P591, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. The fifth document, tab 5, the document mentioned at paragraph 40 of the 92 ter statement, 65 ter number 7287.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Can you confirm, Witness, that this document is dated 22nd of October, 1991, and that it bears your signature?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Is it a document where we have a detailed report about the number of -- about the deaths for that particular period of time, from August 25th to October 21st, 1991?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Same question as with the previous document, was this document sent by fax?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I seek to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have the same question for you as before, Witness. We have a document here that describes a rather serious situation, a terrible situation. You're talking about dead people, you're talking about wounded people. Did the European Mission call you back to tell them that they would take the necessary steps or is it so that no one called you back?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, nobody called.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. No one called you. I see in this document something that I find rather interesting. You're saying that three JNA soldiers were wounded, and you give their names: Sergeant Sasa Jovic, who apparently is a member of VP 4795, a unit from Belgrade. So, unless I'm mistaken, in your hospital, members of the JNA who had been wounded received treatment as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And you also provided medical treatment to injured personnel from the Croatian Army. Fine. We'll come back to that issue later. We need a number for this document now, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P592, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me move on to the sixth document, Witness, at tab 6, mentioned at paragraph 41; 65 ter number 7294.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Witness, is this a document dated 27th of October, 1991, and signed by yourself?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: This is a document related to admissions at the hospital on that particular day and to the number of injured at the hospital? Was this document sent by fax?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I seek to tender this document, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This document relates to the situation on the 27th of October, 1991. It is addressed to the EC Mission. Did they call you back or did nothing happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: You confirm that you got no response to this fax; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Do you know if any other action was taken by the European Commission's Monitoring Mission vis a vis the Serb forces who were surrounding Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. I had daily contacts with the Minister of Health, Professor Hebrang, who told me there were negotiations going on in the European Mission, that they were to go their best to bring about a cessation of bombing of the hospital, but nobody called me from the European Mission and I don't know what their activities were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Did Professor Hebrang tell you or inform you otherwise that the information that you had provided through these faxes was effectively communicated to the European Commission's Monitoring Mission and discussed and taken into account? Did you know, in other words, if your messages were ever received by the ECMM?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He told me they were doing everything to help the Vukovar Hospital, but I have no confirmation myself as to what anyone from the ECMM had done about my faxes. I suppose - in fact, I'm sure - they were well informed, and I learned, indeed after the war, that they had sufficient information. Apart from that, through that liaison office of the ECMM in Croatia, I sent faxes not only to the mission itself but to the politicians who were then the big players in Europe and the world. Later, in the documents, you'll probably see whom exactly I had called and informed, and I got all these fax numbers from the liaison office of the ECMM. So apart from informing the ECMM, I also sent faxes directly to those telephone and fax numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I understand that. My question was, however, if you are certain that the information that you provided to the Mission and to the politicians was ever received by the recipients. Did this information get through to them, and was it taken into account when they negotiated? Do you know that? If you don't know, then just say so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it did, this information reached them. At the time when I was sending the faxes, I did not get any confirmation. But later after the war, in contacts with some of those people, specifically with Mr. Chenu, who was the president of the European Mission at the time, I learned that they certainly had that information and that it had helped them to do something about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: That's exactly what I wanted to know. Thank you very much, Madam.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Registrar, can we have a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P593, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Let me now move to the seventh document, to be found at tab 7, the document mentioned at paragraph 42 of the 92 ter statement, and the 65 ter number of the document is 7302.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Witness, could you confirm that this document is dated 2nd of November, 1991, and that this document bears your signature?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you briefly tell us what this document is about?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Well, I tried, like in all those days, to describe what happened that day. The hospital was targeted by heavy artillery and air bombs every day. On that particular day, one of our employees who went to the door of the boiler room got killed; Ivan Ragus was his name. There were several incidents that day. One reservist, Markovic, Aleksandar, had been brought that day wounded. He was brought by Croatian soldiers, and he was admitted. At any rate, I tried to inform not only the ECMM but all the relevant factors about what happened that day, to give them an update.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you confirm that this document was sent by fax or not?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I seek to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we look at the addressees, we see Admiral Brovet, President Tudjman, Minister Hebrang, General Tus, and the EC Mission, but who did you fax this document to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Again, the ECMM and the Ministry of Health. Those are the numbers to which I sent these faxes, because I sent them myself. I expected that they would forward my faxes to the other addresses if they possibly can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Who is Admiral Brovet?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to the information I had then, he was the commander of the armed forces in the territory of the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But how did you send this letter to Admiral Brovet, through whom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Again, I sent it to the ECMM, hoping that they would forward it to all the others, because I was repeating myself. In this information, I also said that members of the Yugoslav Army were involved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The problem, Witness, is that the EC Mission might have believed that you had sent the same document to Brovet, Tudjman, Hebrang, and Tus, because we see at the end of the document: "Send to." So they could have thought that you had sent the document to these people yourself. They might not have understood that they needed to forward this letter to these high-ranking officials. That's the way we read the letter, because in your own language, you wrote: "Dostaviti," and I suppose it means "Addressees." Very well. We're going to give a number to this document.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P594, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Dutertre.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Let me now move to the eighth document at tab 8, a document mentioned at paragraph 43, 65 ter number 7338; paragraph 43, 65 ter number 7338.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Is this document dated the 3rd of November, 1991, and signed by yourself?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Is this document related to admissions at the hospital on the 2nd of November, 1991, on the preceding day?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Once again, same question: Was this document sent by fax?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I seek to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, here we have a document that is addressed to no one. We don't see any addressee mentioned on this document. Could you please tell us what was the purpose of this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was sent again to the liaison office of the ECMM, and the situation I described was really, really hard. I did not have time, every time, to repeat everything. My purpose was to write this information as quickly as possible and to have it circulated as widely as possible. The people were completely besieged, and my purpose was to inform everyone of what was going on in Vukovar, and this information is dated November 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. A number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P595, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Witness, let me now move to the ninth document at tab 9, the document mentioned at paragraph 44 of the 92 ter statement, 65 ter number 7309. Is this document dated 9th of November, 1991, and does it bear your signature?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: What is this document about? What do you say in this document?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Well, the first thing I want to say is there is a mistake. It says "9th October"; it was, in fact, November. I was explaining, again, what was going on at the hospital, which was constantly being shelled and targeted by various other devastating projectiles. One of our employees had a premature delivery that day. I wanted, in fact, clearly to show what the situation was like; that we had no water, that incendiary grenades were being thrown at us, that the yard of the hospital was on fire, the roof of the hospital as well, and things were harder and harder with every day. The Yugoslav Army and all those following it had decided to completely destroy the town and everything in it. I wanted to show in this way what exactly was going on at the hospital and around it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Can you confirm that this document was sent by fax to the liaison office of the European Mission, as mentioned at paragraph 44 of your 92 ter statement?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I seek to tender this document, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, in this document, you mention the delivery of a premature child weighing 800 grams. Did this child survive?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. No, he didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. A number, please, for this document.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P596, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Madam, who was this letter addressed to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The liaison office of the ECMM in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Witness, let me now move to the 10th document to be found at tab 10, mentioned at paragraph 58 of your 92 ter statement, and bearing 65 ter number 7339. Witness, what is the date of this document?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: This copy, which is in the English language, one can assume that it is the 18th of November.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Who signed the document, if you know?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Professor Andrija Hebrang, signed on behalf of the Republic of Croatia; and in the right-hand side of this document, as far as I can see, that is Andrija Raseta and Georges-Marie Chenu; although that is not clearly written here. I had not seen this document while I was in Vukovar, but only after having exited it. And according to the information I have, those persons -- it is the signatures of those persons that are on this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: This was the question I was about to ask you. You saw this document only later, and you said, "... after I left." What do you mean? Can you tell us, leaving, what departure you're mentioning?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: On the 20th of November, I was arrested and taken to prison, first in Sremska Mitrovica and then also to the Military Investigation Prison in Belgrade, and I was exchanged as a prisoner of war. So it was only after my arrival in Zagreb that I started to investigate what had happened during all those days, during the evacuation period, given the fact that a very large number of staff, medical staff, wounded, and civilians from the hospital from Vukovar never appeared in Croatia and they were all registered as missing persons. At that time, we did not know exactly where people were. In prison, I could see that there were many people from Vukovar and that there were also wounded persons in the prison. I didn't know who they were. I hoped that they were from the hospital. But later, when I collected the testimonies of all those who had arrived in Croatia, we actually established that only a number of the wounded had been evacuated on the convoy, 174 of them, into the free part of Croatia, and that some 250 wounded were missing. On the basis of all these testimonies, we later investigated where they could be, and there is a document already on that particular subject in this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: So this was after you were liberated; only then could you see this document. What is this document about, Witness? What is the purpose of it?
