utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: As far as I could gather later, when I studied it, its purpose was -- were to be rules as to how the hospital was to be evacuated, that it would be neutralised, and that taking a certain path, all the wounded, all the medical staff, and all the people from the Vukovar Hospital would be evacuated. The signatures of these persons who at that time were relevant persons actually say that this was a document of international significance because it was addressed to the European Mission in the presence of the International Red Cross, which was to be also present alongside the European Monitors during the evacuation of the hospital. We hoped until the last day that that would, indeed, happen like that, but as is well known, it did not, and this agreement was not fully applied in practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Witness. I seek to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you appraised yourself of this document after you had been detained, yourself, and this document, in my view, raises a host of problems. I'd like to know what you think about them. You have just said that this document was signed in the very premises of the ECMM; but in this document, I fail to see any mention anywhere of the ECMM. So how could the ECMM sponsor this or be a player in drafting this agreement whilst it's not even mentioned in the text? Because as I've looked at Article 1, I can see the people or the ones that represented, Croatia, JNA, Red Cross, Medecins Sans Frontieres, and the Maltese Red Cross, but I can't see ECMM. So how do you account for that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not think that I'm able to explain that, in fact. We would have to ask the people who were in charge of the ECMM at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A second observation: This document was signed by the Republic of Croatia, so I suppose it was signed by Minister Hebrang, as you indicated, and by a representative of the JNA. It must have been General Raseta. Above that, we see a signature but we don't know whose it is. Is that the signature of somebody representing MSF or the ICRC? We don't know. Who signed above the two signatures?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to the information I have, it was Georges-Marie Chenu, the president of the ECMM, but this is what I heard. I cannot claim that with certainty. He was the organiser of that meeting, and he is a signatory, in view of the fact that the ICRC was to evacuate the -- to organise the evacuation, but I'm not sure because I did not attend that meeting myself. It was in Zagreb, and I was in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you think that it was this Frenchman, who headed the European Mission, who signed; although, we can't see any mention of the ECMM. So we see something, but we don't even know whose signature it is. It may be his. However, we can see several other participants, at least the Red Cross, the ICRC, Medecins Sans Frontieres, and we can't see any signature representing them. Can you shed some light on this or don't you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the only thing I know is what Professor Hebrang had told me; that they were all anxious to help the evacuation of the hospital and that they were working to figure out a way how to come to Vukovar from two sides: One would be by the land route and the second by a tunnel from Hungary, with this also owned by the Maltese order. They wanted to help evacuate the hospital via the Danube. I did not believe that to be possible, and I thought that at that moment it was, in fact, inadequate because all the wounded were in a very grave condition and needed to be evacuated as quickly as possible in ambulances to the first, normal, safe hospitals which had the conditions for their further treatment, rather than being aboard a boat and travel the Danube, and so on and so forth. But they tried to help us in every possible way and to help bring about the cessation of the devastation of Vukovar and of the hospital. So I believe that that was one of the ways in which they were trying to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as you know, can Professor Hebrang speak English?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What about General Raseta?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's have a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P597, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Dutertre. The next document.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, number 11. We're now moving on to the issue of identification of lists of victims. That is a concern. It's mentioned at paragraph 0123; its 65 ter number 7280. We have coloured copies. I'm about to have them distributed, because you had black-and-white copies, unfortunately, in the binders that you received. Mr. Usher, can you help. We'd like the accused and the Trial Chamber to receive copies with colours, but it can be up-loaded in e-court whilst I'm speaking, in colours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Witness, under tab 10, we have a document. What is its source?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the witness has said that she wished documents containing medical information to be held confidentially, so maybe we should move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, let us move to private session for questions of medical files. Madam Registrar, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Madam Registrar, the previous document is to be admitted under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, it will be under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Document number 12, mentioned at paragraph 124. It is 65 ter document 7281, to be found at tab 12. Let's look at the first page. The ERN number is 0469-3283.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: What is this document about? What is this list?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: This is a list of people who, according to the evidence of other people who had made statements, had been, on the 20th November, in Vukovar Hospital; but after that date, they had not been heard from or found. At that time, they were still not identified or found anywhere as killed. They were on record as missing.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters kindly ask all microphones to be switched off, all other microphones.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Let's turn to the following page, 0469-3284, 3285, and 3286; 3284 to 3286.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: What is this list about?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: This is a list of people who were in the Vukovar Hospital on the 20th November and whose remains were later identified at Ovcara. Those were wounded people who had been killed and later identified as killed at Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that we'll find out how the identification was conducted with Witness Strinovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Witness, did you take part in compiling these two lists?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: I did, because the last time I appeared here as a witness, when I was coming here as a witness, I wanted to establish the identities of the wounded people as distinguished from the employees of the hospital and other civilians exhumed at Ovcara. These other civilians that had been taken away from the Vukovar Hospital for some other reasons; that is to say, there were some people who were seen at the Vukovar Hospital on the 20th November, but their remains were not found in the mass grave at Ovcara, and we still don't know where they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Could you tell us who else contributed to compiling these two lists, apart from you?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: My team at the Vukovar Hospital, which among other things deals with the investigation of events of 1991, in the projects we are involved in, gathered information from various associations, such as the Mothers of Vukovar who published a book about the captured and missing, sons and husband; then there is also the Association of Former Inmates of Concentration Camps and another association in the health department. Our purpose was to describe every person who had been identified at Ovcara with a larger number of parameters than just name and surname.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Fine. When you talk about the database of the health ministry, you're talking about the database we mentioned earlier on. The following documents are forms with photographs. Can you tell us what these documents are about? What are these documents?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Those are forms that we filled in and sent to the information staff of the health ministry. It contains name and surname, father's name, date of birth, diagnosis, location of wounding, and whether the person was sent on to another hospital or not. There is a questionnaire to be filled in for every patient, and it is included in this database. Additionally, we included a short CV and a photograph that we found in the documents collected by governmental organisations in order to present to this Court exactly who these people were, because it is different from the test documents we normally have with just name and surname. You can see how many people, including the elderly, the very young, civilians, who are killed at Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. I seek to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a number of questions to put to you with respect to that document, Witness. Please turn to the list of missing persons, 45 in total. So if I understand correctly, to this day, these persons are still missing.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. At that time when this list was made, they were not yet found. Whether they have been found in the meantime, I would have to inquire. This is information available on the date of the compilation of this document. I know some people personally from this list, and I know they have not been found.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may assist the Chamber, Witness Bilic will deal with the matter of people still missing today. This information will be provided to you, updated information. Speaking from memory, I believe we are talking about 53 individuals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's have a look at number 2 on the list, Bozak, Ivan. He was a member of the War Hospital. That's what we read here. Your hospital, was it a civilian hospital or a war hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Our hospital was a civilian hospital before the war. However, when the war began and the aggression in Vukovar started, we treated both civilians and people who were wounded in the war like all other hospitals in Croatia, especially those who were close to the frontline. At that time, all of them were war hospitals. This man, Ivan Bozak, under number 2, he was actually a receptionist; and on the 20th November, he was alive when the army came in - I mean the Yugoslav Army and all the other paramilitary troops - but he was not heard from or seen again. His remains were not found or identified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. You'll probably help me to understand the following: Number 3, Baketa, Goran; number 22, Drago Krizan; number 31, Josip Mikletic; number 35, Perkovic, Tihomir; and number 38, Samardzic, Damjan. Next to their names, we the word "Security." Did you have guards at the hospital, guards from the MUP, because for number 3, we see "MUP, Hospital Security." So did you have people there in charge of providing security for the hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were people who were designated by the commander of the defence to provide security to the hospital. They were from the police, and they are indicated as "MUP," and somewhere from the town defence staff. I thought personally there was not much point in that, because the hospital was completely encircled and shelled and bombed every day, and they certainly could not provide any security against that. But it's sure that these people were assigned. This Goran Baketa was taken away. He was never seen again, live or dead. Then, again, Branko Lukenda, his job, he was assigned by the police to make a record of the wounded and to collect weapons from the wounded who were brought to the hospital and take these weapons to the police. This Damjan Samardzic was assigned to the hospital apparently to secure the wounded JNA soldiers. It was said of him that he was so badly beaten at Ovcara by the paramilitaries that he died, but he is on this list because he has not been identified in the mass grave. There are witnesses, however, claiming that he was beaten up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me interrupt you, Witness. The person is identified as belonging to a security. I suppose they had weapons. They provided security to the hospital, and to do so they had weapons, or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They did not have any weapons in the hospital. They had a small room where they put their weapons in storage; but inside the building, they were all unarmed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me turn to the second list, including 97 persons exhumed from the mass grave. They had been admitted into the hospital or they were in the hospital; and later on, their bodies were exhumed. Can you confirm that there were 97 of them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. And in the rest of the document, we have certificates where various injuries are described. For example, for Drazen Babic, we know that he was a guard; and when looking at these certificates, it's something I did earlier on, we find that the majority of these people were soldiers. To your knowledge, Witness, how many civilian staff members of the hospital were killed or disappeared? How many? Can you give us a figure, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Eighteen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Eighteen. And amongst these 18 individuals, none of them were ever found?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. Two were never found, two are missing. The impression I have, and I may be mistaken, and if I'm mistaken, tell me so, when I look at these certificates relating to these 97 persons, I have a feeling that the majority of them were military personnel. But for some of them, we see that they are identified as being civilians; for example, Franjo Barisic, adult civilian. That's what we read. To your knowledge, how many civilians died after having been arrested and taken to the Ovcara farm? To your knowledge or according to you, how many civilians were killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you see, it's hard to say, because many are still recorded as missing, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you give us a ballpark figure?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But, roughly speaking, about 50 per cent were civilians, because if you look at this list of the wounded, you see, for instance, some of our employees, such as Dragan Gavric, driver, and Sinisa Glavlasevic, who was a journalist, are there. So many are actually civilians, certainly half of them were civilians. There were some women, some children. There were three minor children.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Witness, let's not confuse matters. What I'm interested in right now is the persons who were killed at Ovcara and whose bodies were found. That's the only thing I'm interested in. Some of these people disappeared, we don't know where they are, so I'm currently reviewing very closely this particular group of individuals. Roughly speaking, because I haven't counted each and every one of them, but the impression I get is that the majority of these people were soldiers, military men, but with just a few civilians, and that's what I wanted you to tell me. In that particular group, how many civilians do we find?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm telling you, you have 97 wounded persons on this list, wounded, and that includes military personnel and civilians who are identified. In total, 200 bodies were exhumed in Ovcara. Out of these 200, 193 were identified, and you will see that later in other documents. So, in further proceedings, you can see exactly how many civilians there were among them, according to more precise data. But regardless of whether there were civilians or Croatian soldiers, the wounded should have been protected under Geneva Conventions. We did not inquire exactly whether a person was a policeman, or a member of the Guard Corps, or a soldier, but these were just wounded people to us, wounded people who were taken away and killed at Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I'm going to deal now with a matter that is probably very painful for you, but I have to raise that matter. Your father is to be found amongst the victims. Can you tell us about the circumstances in which he was arrested, and can you give us some additional information about all this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In fact, I wanted to correct you earlier. It's not my father, it's my father-in-law; that is, my husband's father.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it should be marked somewhere, "father-in-law."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My father-in-law and my mother-in-law, that's his wife.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. It's your father-in-law. He has the name of your husband, Bosanac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Bosanac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your father-in-law, who was the father of your husband, why was he there, in what capacity? Was he a civilian? Was he a military man?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He was a civilian. He was an old and sick man. He was born in 1919. The day before, he was brought to the hospital with his wife in order to be evacuated. At my request to place them closer to me, and my mother was also at the hospital at the time, they were, indeed, placed close to me. But that morning, he went outside because it was very difficult for him to sit for a long time, he had problems with his legs, and he just went out to stretch his legs. But as soon as he got outside, he was put on the bus to Ovcara, and nobody ever saw him again. I heard from some survivors of Ovcara that he had been seen there, and he was identified along with all the others in 1996. He was killed there, and he was an old civilian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. We're going to have a break, but just before that, one question. We have another Bosanac on that list. Who is that person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Tomislav Bosanac. It's my husband's nephew. That's a relative. The father of this Tomislav and my father-in-law were brothers, and Tomislav's wife was a nurse who was very seriously wounded, and he was with her. I personally asked Sljivancanin if this relative of mine, Tomislav, could stay with his wife during the evacuation, but he was still taken out that morning, taken to Ovcara, and killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Was Tomislav Bosanac a civilian or a military man?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Civilian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He was a civilian. All right. We are now going to have a break until 12.00 noon. We'll resume at 12.00 and stop at five to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The court is back in session. Mr. Prosecutor, you're seeking to tender document 7281?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please give us a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P599, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Dutertre.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very briefly, three issues. We have the 92 ter statement. The last sentence of paragraph 1, names of relatives of the witness are mentioned there. I don't think that needs to be made public. Is it possible to redact the last sentence of paragraph 1? Equally, at paragraph 123 that deals with the document exhibited under seal, it should be redacted, in my view; and at the earliest convenience, the OTP will provide you with a redacted version of the 92 ter statement. The second point, very briefly. On page 60, line 19, I'd asked Dr. Bosanac whether the database she had mentioned was the one that had been previously used. She said, "Yes," but that had not been recorded in the transcript, so I wanted to mention that. Let me move to the next documents. I will soon be over.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Witness, you said that 200 bodies had been exhumed at Ovcara and that 193 bodies had been identified.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us move to tab 14, mentioned at paragraph 126, 65 ter number 7340.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: My question is as follows: Witness, is this the updated list of individuals identified in the Ovcara mass grave?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: What list are you asking me about now? It is not arranged in that order here in the binder. Are you talking about list 97?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Sorry. Look at the smaller binder, please. It is behind tab 14. It should be on your right-hand side. Tab 14.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Yes, that is that list.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Where does this list come from? Who provided it to you?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: When you got in touch with me, telling me of your intention for me to testify in this case, like last time, I again asked the government of the Republic of Croatia, namely, the Ministry of War Veterans, Family Affairs, and Inter-Generational Solidarity, the Administration for Detainees, for a new updated list of identified persons. So it was on the 28th of August, 2008, that I received a telefax message, and this contained this latest list with 193 persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Would you mind repeating the number? I heard something else in French. I heard "192." Is it 192 or is it 193 identified individuals?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: 193. 192 was the last time when I was here as a witness. That was, I believe, in 2005. The number then was 192. In the meantime, another person has been identified.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Very well. This list of 97 names that we discussed earlier on, is it the list of these people mentioned in this list of 193 individuals about which you say that they'd been wounded and had been admitted into the hospital?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Yes, these are the same persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I seek to tender this document, 7340 -- sorry, I'm just checking the number: 7280.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I had a thorough look at the names, at the 193 names, and I noted that there were some who were under age; in other words, men aged 16 or 17. An example, we have number 82, Igor Kacic, born on the 23rd of August, 1975. What had these people, young people, doing in the hospital? Had he been wounded, was be sick, had he been admitted, brought to hospital? How do you account for his presence there; could you tell me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can do that because I know this young man personally. His father, Petar Kacic, went to school with me, and he was a defender of Vukovar, a member of the Croatian Army. He was killed, and his minor son, Igor, was with his mother in the cellar of the building. On one occasion when there was shelling, a wall crumbled and collapsed on him. He was wounded, so he was at the hospital with his mother, waiting for evacuation. However, he was taken away and killed at Ovcara, even though he was a minor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that in this list of 193 people, he was the youngest of them all, wasn't he? Can you confirm this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, I think that he was, but I believe, actually, that there were some who were even younger, born in 1975, I believe. A minor was killed who was also the son of a woman who worked in our laundry, and his name is Balog, Dragutin Balog. He was born on the 19th of August, 1974, he was the son of a woman working in our laundry room, and he was together with his father who had throat cancer. They were with his mother, who was working at the hospital, and they were all waiting for the evacuation. Both of them, the husband, i.e., the father of this minor son, so the father and son were both taken to Ovcara and killed there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we have a number for this list, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P600, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Let us move to document 15 mentioned at paragraph 126.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You skipped 13?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. It had some historic value in terms of chronology, but I wanted to save time. That's the 1992 list that has not yet been updated. I didn't think it was necessary to have it in the file. I should have said so. So document 15, mentioned at paragraph 126, 65 ter number 7341.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Witness, can you please confirm that this has been initialled and that this document bears the date of the 23rd of September, 2008?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's tab 15. Could the usher help the witness with tab 15.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: So we have again the list of 97 individuals, but, as it were, updated, based on the update of the people identified at Ovcara, that list of 193 names; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: So this is the latest update, even though there were no changes?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please be asked to speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I seek to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a technical question for you, Witness. With regard to this list of 97 names, I'm looking at the column of "Diagnosis." For each name, we have a specification. Is this the postmortem diagnosis or was this the diagnosis at the time of admission? Can you please tell us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These diagnoses were made during the hospitalisation of the people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So this is not a diagnosis arising from the autopsies, following exhumation. This is the reason why these individuals were admitted into hospital. For instance, we have an example, number 14, this person had been wounded by explosion; is that so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Prosecutor, you wanted a number. Let's have one.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P601, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Let's move to document 16, and I'm not going to deal with document 17. Document 16 is to be found under tab 16, it is mentioned at paragraph 127, 65 ter number 7319.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Witness, would you mind reading out, so that it can be translated, the heading of this document, starting with the word "Prilog." I'll spare you the rest. I really have an appalling accept in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Yes, it says: "Victims from the farm of Ovcara from the Vukovar Hospital."

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For your information, Your Honours, this is an exhibit admitted in the Mrksic case, based on the list of victims as mentioned in the Mrksic case.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Witness, could you tell us who wrote the handwritten mentions that we have in front of each and every name of this list?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: In agreement with the Prosecutor, Mr. Moore, I put that in. He wanted me to describe from memory, not only me but other witnesses as well, in relation to these names, what we knew about them; whether they were Croatian soldiers, political enemies, workers at the hospital. Then using these signs, we tried to write, all of us, everything that we knew about. For instance, for me, this asterisk here means that he worked at a hospital. For instance, Ilija Asadjanin, he has been marked as a member of the hospital staff. So I marked -- I put a mark by the name and put what I knew about them. But the interpretation was done by someone from the OTP. It is not mine, those interventions; namely, they explain what these markings and the letters meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Well, you are ahead of me. You've already answered my next question. Thank you for that. More specifically, could you tell us what all these signs mean? I'll be more specific. When you write a "C" in front of a name, what does that letter "C" mean?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: "C" means "Civilian." It is indicated there in the legend, in the explanation given with the list. "W" means "Political animal" [as interpreted] which is for those that I knew were perhaps political enemies of the then-Yugoslav option. It was Mr. Moore's idea to try and pinpoint the reason why precisely those people had been taken away to Ovcara and killed there; although, I personally feel that it is pointless -- and felt it was pointless to analyse matters in that fashion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So there's a mistake in the transcript on page 74, line 5. "W" stands for "Political enemies" and not "animal."

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Quite so, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, I have an objection. Mr. Presiding Judge, it is not a mistake in the transcript, because the witness did say "political animal," which means "political animal." She's trying to speech English, and she doesn't have a clue in English. She should have said "Political enemy," but she did say "animal." I heard it very well, and I laughed to myself when I heard it. She said "animal."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Dr. Bosanac, did you say that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said quite clearly "political enemy."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Anyway, we've got the soundtrack. We can check. So you said "political enemy," but how do you know that these were political opponents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I knew in respect of some. In respect of many, I didn't know, and I said so in respect of those people, that I knew that was the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me take an example, that of Ivan Bainrauh. You wrote that he was -- well, who was he? Was he an opponent or not? This is number 8 in the list.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I know. I can see that. I can't be sure. I wrote it because I thought that he was a political opponent, but I wasn't sure. I marked him anyway because I thought that he was, but I really thought that not relevant as a method of analysis. I just tried to mark the people that I -- whom I knew with the signs given me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So political opponents to whom, to what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I suppose that they belonged to this option which actually led to the aggression on Vukovar. That is at least how I understood the Prosecutor Moore. Perhaps it would be better if you asked him what he had meant precisely when he asked us to mark these things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So he asked you to indicate whether, among the victims, there were opponents, people opposed to the aggression on Vukovar. So Prosecutor Moore concluded that that person was a political opponent, and you continued by indicating "W," but apparently you regret that move now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't regret it, but I just think that it wasn't of the essence, that it wasn't relevant. I put all these question marks because I was not sure what mark to put. I thought even then it pointless to actually mark and divide the victims in that way, but Prosecutor Moore asked me to do it in that way, so I did the best I could.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, the mere fact that the Prosecutor is asking you something does not mean that you have to do what he tells you to or asks you to. You are absolutely independence, regardless of whether the Judges, the accused, or the Prosecution ask you to do something. So it was the Prosecutor, you say, who'd asked you to write this down. Let me take another example on page 2, Ivan Bozak. That's the first name on page 2. Did you know him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I knew him. He was our doorman, and "WH" is placed by his name, meaning "Work hospital," meaning that he was on the hospital staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So he was a civilian employee in the hospital. Please proceed, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: So when you marked the letter "S," which is "V" in B/C/S, what does that mean when you write that in front of an "M"?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: "S," according to the legend here, means "Soldier," so he was a soldier, and I put that mark by the name so those whom I knew to be soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Fine. When we see a star or a "WH," can you remind us what category of people that represents?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: That refers to the hospital staff, the workers of the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: I see. Then when we see a cross and then "HWH"?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: These are auxiliary staff at the hospital, those who are not professional medical staff but were auxiliary staff. For instance, the husbands of the nurses who worked there came there to work as assistants in different ways.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Thank you. And when you don't know, you just put a question mark; is that so?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: After you did all this, did you have enough time to check it all? What I mean to say is that this matches your memory, well, to the best of your knowledge. What is the degree of certainty we can attribute to this information?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: It is a quite high degree of certainty, but I should like to say that these markings reflect my view of those people, what I knew about them. I cannot say that it was something certain. The Prosecutor asked me to indicate my view of persons at the hospital. I suppose that he also asked the other witnesses to do the same. Now, whether it really is precise, I can't say. I believe that a much more precise piece of information is the one which is contained in the database of the information staff of the health ministry, where the data indicates whether someone was a Croatian soldier, a police member, or a civilian. In this list, it is only there that we can obtain more details. In this list, we can only see whether someone came to assist at the hospital, to work in the kitchen, or perhaps, as I said, they were the husbands of nurses already working at the hospital who came to help.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I seek to tender this document, and I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have a number for this document, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P602, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Witness, I told you earlier that I have a number of questions to put to you. I'm going to try to proceed in a logical fashion. But before doing so, let me put this technical question to you. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You told us, and the documents have shown it, you've told us that in this hospital, you would provide treatment to wounded people, whether they were Serbs or Croatians. To the best of your recollection, at some point in time did you have, in your hospital, a Serb fighter who was not a member of the JNA but who was either a volunteer or a reservist? Did you have to deal with such a situation, having to treat a patient, a Serb, who was not a member of the JNA? Can you provide some specifics? Can you provide us with a specific example?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: I remember that day there was a reservist who came as a volunteer. He was wounded and brought to our hospital, but I can't remember his name. All I know is that happened a few times.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And you, yourself, did you talk to these, quote/unquote, "volunteers"? Did you speak with these people?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you ask them what they were doing there? Why they were there? What did they tell you?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: I did not ask them that because they were seriously wounded, and they were people not capable of answering such questions at that time. I did not try to talk to them about that. I only spoke to those people whom I described in my appeals, and they were people who had been re-convalescing for a long time. Their ward was hit by a shell, and I just asked them to put their signature to my fax to confirm that all of it is true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is something that I find rather confusing, a topic I find rather confusing. It's the topic of the JNA wounded. We can very well picture in our minds the situation in Vukovar, Vukovar under siege, wounded people on the streets, and so on and so forth. But what about JNA personnel who were wounded, who would bring them to the hospital? How would it happen, practically speaking?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Those who were brought to the hospital were brought by Croatian troops who were on the frontline, and they brought those wounded to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In other words, during fighting, wounded Serbs who had been captured by Croatian soldiers would be taken to the hospital by Croatian soldiers. You say that with certainty. From memory, are we talking about a lot of people, a lot of such cases during that period? Are we talking about one or two individuals, several dozens? How many wounded Serb soldiers received treatment at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: I remember, in August, four of them were brought. That was at the beginning; and then later another three, then another two, then another two. I'd have to think back to answer this question, to remember all these details.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. So there was a number of them. I suppose that all necessary steps had been taken at the hospital for these wounded Serb soldiers, who were also prisoners, for them to be under guard and not to be mistreated?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: I told you before that this man, Samardzic, had been sent by the defence commander to guard these soldiers. While there were three of them, they were in a separate room.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters cannot hear anything from the extra microphones on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] However, their ward was hit by a shell, and, fortunately, nobody was hurt that time. But after that shell, they were placed together with the other wounded Croatian soldiers and civilians.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to address the period before the attack of Vukovar by the JNA. With your help, I'd like us to go back in time. At paragraph 8 of your written statement, you say that there were 45.000 inhabitants in Vukovar, there were different ethnic groups, Croats, Serbs, and so on and so forth. Before these events in Vukovar, was there a quiet atmosphere amongst all the ethnic groups or were there clear tensions between these groups?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Well, everybody has a different perception of that, I suppose. I personally spent my entire life in Vukovar and had worked for 17 years as a physician. Before the war in Vukovar, I was never involved in politics. But the fact is tensions began in Yugoslavia even just after the -- after Tito's death, and things got worse with various movements in Vojvodina, in Croatia. What happened in Croatia happened on the 18th of August, 1991, when roadblocks were put up, and the Croatian Assembly announced the decision to declare Croatia's independence after a referendum. To the best of my knowledge, there had been negotiations about transforming Yugoslavia into something like a confederation; and according to that idea, the republics should have become confederal units. But at that time, this idea didn't pass because the policy of Greater Serbia, pursued by Slobodan Milosevic, put an end to these negotiations, and the Yugoslav Army was the extended arm of that Greater Serbia policy. I'm telling you I wasn't involved in politics, I was an outside observer, and it's a fact that in those border areas of Croatia, we felt that something was wrong and that it is not guaranteed that peace would be preserved. However, when the Log Revolution, as it was called, started in Pakrac, in that part of Vojvodina, we did not suspect that things would end that way, because we had always been a multi-ethnic community. People lived together and had respect for each other, and we simply couldn't believe it. However, it is a fact that paramilitary units arrived in Serbian villages in 1990, the villages around Vukovar. They armed the Serbian population of these villages, they were present at various rallies, and they kept inciting the Serbian people against Croatia. Still, we kept hoping for a political solution, until the 2nd of May, when Croatian policemen were killed in a Serbian village. And after the shelling of Vukovar started, we realised that there would be no peaceful end to this, and I tried to open people's eyes to this through all my communications, all my appeals, to let the world know what this policy is doing to us. These policy-makers were using the Yugoslav Army as a tool to implement the idea of Greater Serbia, it was inconceivable how they could treat people the way they did, but that was the truth; and no one at that time, not even the International Community, the Europe, or the UN, wanted to look the problem in the face. After I was released from the camp, I travelled a lot, and I faced a lot of those politicians who at that time had had the power to do something, and I realised that they had not had enough political will. They wanted to keep Yugoslavia as it was. They let themselves be manipulated by Slobodan Milosevic and the followers of this Great Serbian policy. If you look at -- but when Vukovar happened and when so many civilians got killed, they couldn't turn a blind eye to this anymore. Then things started happening in Bosnia, including Srebrenica; and regardless of all that happened, whether anyone can understand it or not, we, the survivors, know what it was all about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like us to review the situation from the perspective of your hospital. When the independence of Croatia was proclaimed, did this have an impact on the municipality of Vukovar and on your hospital, or did it have no impact whatsoever?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Well, depends from person to person. In spring 1991, we had local elections, and that was the first multi-party election that produced a local government. So the first local elections were in the spring of 1991, and it was a multi-party political system in play for the first time. I believe there were six or seven political parties taking part, and they elected to a multi-party government, a multi-party local assembly, and local government. For instance, Slavko Dokmanovic was elected, although the Serbian Party was not even registered by then. It was registered only after the elections led by Jovan Raskovic. But at those elections, Slavko Dokmanovic was on the ticket of the Communist Party or some other party; whereas, another man, Mr. Soldo, was elected head of the local government. And at the local level, these political parties tried to agree about the distribution of power. However, later, when these proponents of the Greater Serbian idea, the Radical Party and the Chetniks and the paramilitaries, it all changed. Slavko Dokmanovic stopped going to work, Marin Vidic was no longer the civilian commissioner for Vukovar, there were blockades of Vukovar and surrounding villages, and political solutions were no longer possible. We were heading for war, and we who were encircled tried to do our best to defend ourselves and survive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, let me cut you off. Here I'm relying on your written statement. In your written statement, you mention the Chetniks. I would like you to tell us, from your own point of view, not from the point of view of Mr. Seselj or the OTP, but in your eyes, what is a Chetnik?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: I heard what "Chetnik" meant. Before the war, my ideas about Chetniks came from books and movies, and these volunteers organised by various organisations were called "Chetniks." When I use the word "Chetnik," I use it to denote members of Serbian paramilitary units whom I came across during the war and during the occupation of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have stated that you met with Serbian paramilitary units. What units are you talking about, and in what way are they different from the JNA? This may seem obvious for you, but the Judges were not on the spot at the time, so they need that information.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: I can only tell you my own opinion, but you can also find out from photos, and there is plenty of photo documentation from that period. I thought of those people as Chetniks. They were disheveled, with long beards, wearing fur hats with cockades on them, aggressive, filled with hate. Those are the people whom I thought of as Chetniks, and you can take photos from that period and you will see that these people answer my description.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you see these people move around Vukovar with your own eyes? Did you see some of them walk around the town?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you saw them, did you have the feeling that they were under control or that they were out of control?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: I think they were under the control of their commanders, because they did have their own commanders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To your knowledge, what about their commander, who was it under the control of?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: I think the chief commander was the accused in this case. I heard that personally when I listened to the Serbian radio while still living in Vukovar, and I read it in literature, which made it obvious that he was one of the highest-ranking commanders of these units. He actually united them all. I remember, when I was giving a statement in the prison in Mitrovica, when a colonel was interrogating me about the burial of the dead while we were still in Vukovar, he asked me to draw a sketch of who was buried where, to the best of my recollection. I told him the best thing to do is to go back to Vukovar and I could show him on the spot, rather than try to remember in prison. He said it was not a good idea at all because the Yugoslav Army had no jurisdiction over that territory anymore, and it was a big question how to get into Vukovar and then get out. That's when I first realised that the Yugoslav Army had no control over these people whatsoever. In fact, the part of the Yugoslav Army that implemented this policy probably had some control. They acted in unison, and it's obvious from many newspaper articles at the time; but at that time, I still didn't know that. I still thought the Yugoslav authority -- the Yugoslav Army had more authority. But it's obvious they were acting together, acting in unison. The link was not completely broken; otherwise, it wouldn't have been possible for the Yugoslav Army to be completely neutral.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After the multi-party elections, a new municipal authority was introduced, and you said that at that time paramilitary units and Chetniks arrived in town. At that specific point in time, at a time when the JNA had done nothing yet, there had been no attack at that time, during that period of time, would you listen to Serbian radio, is that what you're saying, and you heard in the news that these Chetniks, these paramilitary units, were coming under the control of Mr. Seselj or X, Y, Z? Did you hear that even before the JNA started shelling the town? But which radio? I suppose there were several radio stations. Which one would you listen to?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: I listened to Novi Sad, Belgrade, Radio Sabac. Those were all stations that we received in our area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, we've had several witnesses here, but -- let me interrupt myself because I'm looking at the clock. We have to adjourn. I'll proceed with my questions tomorrow, but rest assured that we'll complete your testimony tomorrow. Tomorrow, we'll start working at a quarter past 2.00. We were supposed to work in the morning initially, but the Appeals Chamber is sitting in the Krajisnik case in the morning, and we were asked if we could sit in the afternoon; whereas, we were scheduled to be working in the morning. The outcome of all this is that we'll meet again tomorrow at 2.15. Please make the necessary arrangements. You've taken the solemn declaration. You are here to testify in the interests of justice. As such, you're not supposed to have any contacts with the OTP, but I'm sure you know that. I will also instruct you not to have any contacts, any dealings, with representatives of the press to talk about your testimony. I hope you understand that. So if you want to call your family, no problem, but do not have any contacts with the media, because you are here to testify for the interests of justice and you're not supposed to have any contacts with anyone about your testimony. We'll adjourn and meet again tomorrow afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 5th day of November, 2008, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 12.56 p.m.,
